"Physical" copies of GTA 6 started shipping out to early buyers this week, including several members of GamesRadar+ staff. As players start to worry that their codes may be stolen with a bizarre flashlight trick, we had to see if we could steal our own – and honestly, I wouldn't be too worried about the possibility.

Rockstar's approach to its code-in-box release of GTA 6 is slightly different from most publishers. Rather than including the game code printed on a slip of paper in the case, the code is printed inside the back cover art itself. Social media is starting to be washed over with reports that if you shine a very bright flashlight just right into the edge of a GTA 6 case, you can make out the code without even breaking the seal on the game.

I tried the trick with my own US copy of the PS5 physical edition, and it did not work. There's a strip of camouflage patterning underneath the code that renders it unreadable from the opposite side no matter how bright a light you shine at it. My colleague Catherine tried the trick with her UK PS5 copy, and same deal – the code is unreadable through that camo pattern.

There is a catch here: not every code-in-box copy of GTA 6 has the camo strip. I've combed through unboxing videos of the game, and while I can't find any examples of US copies without the protective camouflage, some copies with a PEGI rating only have a plain black strip in the background. This, it seems, is the one that could be vulnerable to the apparent flashlight trick.

However, I haven't managed to track down anybody reporting that they've fallen victim to a stolen code. Most retailers keep their games behind locked glass cases, so a prospective code thief would probably have to buy the game, hope that it's a black background version, get an unusually powerful flashlight, shine it in, and then convince the retailer to take the game back for a refund in order for anyone to fall afoul of the potential scam.

Is that a level of trouble anyone's willing to go to in order to play GTA 6 for free? Well, yeah, I guess so. But it's also not an issue unique to GTA's code-in-box release – I've had a few occasions where I've purchased a new, "sealed" copy of a traditional physical game only to find that someone had carefully snuck the disc out of the package and returned it to the retailer where I eventually bought it.

And, well, if you're that worried, you can just buy the game digitally. Yeah, I know, I'm the exact kind of sicko who bought the physical version to have a box on my shelf and a poster on my wall, but it's not as if there's a real difference between getting the box and just doing a digital GTA 6 pre-order. Now, if there was actually a map in the box, that might be a different story.

#3762. How to unlock Flounder and Sebastian in Disney Dreamlight Valley The Keepsake Sea

The collection of characters from The Little Mermaid is growing, with Ariel’s beloved fish friends Flounder and Sebastian joining the village in Disney Dreamlight Valley. The process for unlocking them looks vastly different from all other villagers, though, and can be tricky to navigate.

If you’re hoping to get every character available to find and meet around the valley, figuring out what needs to be done to recruit these two is essential. Here’s how to unlock Flounder and Sebastian in Disney Dreamlight Valley.

Flounder and Sebastian can be unlocked by purchasing either the Deluxe Edition or the Ultimate Edition of The Keepsake Sea in DDV. These two Adventure Companions are exclusive content locked behind these special variants of the Expansion Pass, which means you must buy one of the two to get them.

With either of these versions purchased, you’ll then be able to unlock Flounder and Sebastian in DDV. These two are likely locked behind a few quests, probably ones that require you to first unlock Ariel and progress through part of The Keepsake Sea’s storyline to learn about Adventure Companions. We’ll provide an update here on all additional unlock requirements once they’re available to tackle.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Flounder and Sebastian will very likely only ever be available as exclusive bonus content unlocked for purchasing either the Deluxe Edition or the Ultimate Edition of The Keepsake Sea DLC. Most other DLCs have had similar exclusivity systems for special game editions, like Sven as an exclusive mount with the Deluxe Edition of Wishblossom Ranch.

All items included in special editions have never been available in any other way. This system has been in place for years, so it’s unlikely to change in the future. This means that the only way to get Flounder and Sebastian in your valley is by buying one of the two DLC game versions that include them.

Flounder and Sebastian are Adventure Companions, not full-on villagers in DDV. This means they act as a hybrid between a Companion and a villager. These special Companions can be given gifts, have daily discussions, and come with their own set of rewards, but are not quite as built out as villagers.

#3761. How Origame Digital are channelling and defacing Lovecraft over a trilogy of "inherently indigenous" anti-fascist games

Revisiting the secretive design of Penguin Colony

Much like the H.P. Lovecraft novella it alternately riffs on and skewers, Penguin Colony takes you to an ancient alien city of crabby cuboid geometry and helical designs – comparable at a glance to Lovecraft's "terraces of every sort of provocative disproportion", but here given strangely everyday, anachronistic-seeming labels, such as "Downtown". Later, you're shown flashes of footage of the streets of Melbourne in Australia - developer Origame Digital's base of operations, and a city built on stolen Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung and Bunurong Boon Wurrung land.

When I first set foot in Downtown, in the unassuming body of a Rockhopper penguin, I thought the broad idea was to satirically redefine modern settlements built by European colonisers as Lovecraftian relics, intrusions from the cosmic beyond. This irony seems most pointed in sections where you steer a group of Māori characters, journeying south to prevent an expedition of German and British Nazi occultists from resurrecting a surviving elder being they call the "one true Aryan king". Playing as one of the Māori voyagers, you witness the cyclopean city as a realm of spectral high rises and square windows, rearing out of a swamp of blood and bone.

I'm only somewhat correct about all this. Penguin Colony's reference points are wide-ranging and precise, with the persona of a disinterested penguin serving partly as a means of critical distance from Lovecraft, and partly, as a kind of camouflage for an extremely complex political artwork. It's easy to treat the game's critique as wholly retrospective - an alternately mocking and outraged investigation of a horror author whose bigotry is often reduced to an apologetic footnote or tinny performative disclaimer, drowned out by dread augurs of tentacles in the dark. It's a test of interpretative rigour, amongst other things, for hasty white European reviewers who might slip and slide past the more elaborate allusions into idle chat about Soulslikes.

Speaking to me over videocall, Origame Digital founder and director Naphtali Faulkner acknowledged the broad objective of reframing colonial cities as unearthly aberrations, cutting against cosier visions of colonised Australian land. "There's a bit of an issue with Australian games, where they tend to be tourism pieces, sometimes," he comments. "Not in a bad way, but they do not bring up the violence of this country, in anything. They will comfortably sidestep that for a lot of reasons – one is, a lot of the families that are affected by that are still around. Is it [a non-indigenous developer's] place to tell that story? No. But also, you have this sort of 'Australiana' stuff happen quite a lot, where it's tin roofs and red dirt, that kind of look you see on a postcard."

Still, Penguin Colony's "first colonial city" isn't just a response to 'Australiana'. It's also a monument to 2b2t, the ancient Minecraft "anarchy" server that is infamous for its vicious player culture, and somewhat admired for the colossal strangeness of its desecrated geography. 2b2t is an incarnation of Mojang's sandbox building sim that is so 'pure' and unsparing in its priorities that license owners Microsoft can't entirely acknowledge it. The server's central spawn has been repeatedly built up, defaced and degraded over 16 years of constant operation, forming a nightmare landscape of lavafalls and Wither holes and floating seas and basalt barricades.

"We took data from that, and we modified it, and made it playable," Faulkner tells me. "We had to subdivide it, and it had more detail and stuff, and really transform it a lot, but the whole thing was: what is 2b2t? It's the most realistic depiction of colonisation in a videogame. When you do Minecraft, it's basically a colonisation simulator where you go extract the trees and stuff but it all magically regrows. 2b2t's only rules are there's no rules, and also nothing respawns. You have the Spawn - the Spawn is the most heart-wrenching thing to look at when you first see it, because you know what Minecraft is in your head, you've seen those rolling green hills, and then to see it basically be destroyed into oblivion, is a very strong emotion."

As an inadvertent digital document of colonialism, 2b2t doesn't offer much hope of reparation and redress. "The only way to build back the Spawn is to go back and replant everything," Faulkner says. "And you know, fix the damage that was done, but we all know what gamers did to it, right? They've done various incursions and things like covering it in lava or water, or making it so that you can't leave without cheats." Still, Faulkner considers it "a fascinating relic of gaming". In general, he is interested in how fiction makers might preserve virtual landscapes that reflect "player-run digital ecosystems of people basically going beyond what the designers thought."

2b2t's presence within Penguin Colony is illustrative of how Origame Digital are using Lovecraft over the course of a planned trilogy of "inherently indigenous" Lovecraftian games – not just rebutting the author's anglophilia and white supremacism, not merely flipping the racial power dynamics so as to "make the indigenous people the skull-measuring scientists", but taking Lovecraft's mythos to unfamiliar places and forcing it to serve a politics that Lovecraft himself would despise.

Faulkner himself came across Lovecraft's work around 15 years ago, having been introduced to it by a university friend. He was unmoved, initially, by the author's descriptions of eldritch threats and incomprehensible dimensions. "You know how Lovecraft's described, with Cthulhu - 'unknowable horror', 'madness inducing'," he says. "And then you see it and it's kind of like an octopus. It's a bit underwhelming." Faulkner grew more intrigued by Lovecraft, however, after seeing other artists adapt his work. He points to the Shadows Over Innsmouth music video created by Carpenter Brut - a contributor to Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's OST - and also, to Victor LaValle's The Ballad of Black Tom, an adaptation of Lovecraft's The Horror at Red Hook written from the perspective of a Black man. "I started to understand that Lovecraft isn't just the author's works," he says. "It's this all-encompassing thing that has inspired so much stuff."

Even as he pondered Lovecraft and the broader, somewhat dissociative genre of the Lovecraftian, Faulkner was also investigating his own heritage as a Ngāi Te Rangi person living in a former British colony, tracing patterns of invasion, conquest and assimilation that, he says, have repeated themselves since the days of the Romans and Vikings. "I think the reason that I decided to do this, was that when I started to get Lovecraft, it was when I was really starting to have the understanding that every indigenous person has at some point about what colonisation is," he says. "You know, where you have to learn your own family history, and you have to learn why things are the way they are at the moment. And so to me, it was like that thing of, when you start seeing Lovecraft as this thing about displacement, invasion, destruction, language - it reached me at the perfect time in my life when I was already looking at this stuff, and I thought that it was a really apt analogy."

Faulkner also sensed that even Lovecraft enthusiasts who are less mindful of the author's politics were yearning for a fresher kind of Lovecraftian fable. "When it comes to indigenous stuff, the thing is that we're not really represented in anything, and our histories are rarely given a platform to say stuff, especially in games," he goes on. "But what I'd sort of looked at with Lovecraft, was that I think fans were ready for it, because people had gotten a little tired of these direct, 1-to-1 adaptations, that still exist in the space of the unknowable horror is unknowable, rather than trying to say, why is the unknowable horror scary?"

The idea of the "unknowable" pervades Lovecraftian fiction, as does the idea of "cosmic indifference", that terror of being engulfed in a vaster universe of forms and forces that barely register the existence of human beings. This "unknowability" is concentrated in the balefully blank gaze of Psurumin, the otherworldly entity at the far end of Penguin Colony - the last Earthly remnant of an empire spanning hundreds of planets. "I stare into its eyes," intones Howard Blakely, the game's English narrator, and an initially unconsenting member of the doomed Nazi expedition. "I stare deep within, and yet I see nothing. I am not even a speck of inane curiosity."

Penguin Colony overlaps this Lovecraftian "cosmic indifference" with Faulkner's grief and bewilderment at how perpetrators of empire have insulated themselves from feelings of responsibility or shame. "For example in the southern hemisphere here, Australia and New Zealand, the idea was that the missionaries would say 'don't worry, we're saving them, we're turning them into Christians, we had to kill the ones who resist'," he says. "And the soldiers that had immense trauma and guilt from doing that would be consulted by a priest and told, 'you were doing it for the greater good'."

"To me it's saying: how could they do that to us?" Faulkner goes on. "What made them do that? To me as a younger person, it was very 'unknowable'. You've probably talked to other indigenous people, I hope, before in your life, and it's this kind of thing especially where there's a lot of pain there, because... how could someone choose to do that? And even to this day, there's a question around even saying sorry about it. Or there's questions around people, they want to sort of move on from history, and never bring it up, never acknowledge it again, whilst the injustice of colonisation is still present."

Howard Blakely is a mirror of sorts for this culture of denial and obfuscation. For all his apparent awareness that Psurumin does not regard him as a fellow being, and that to release the creature would be calamitous, he succumbs to the idea that he can ship the starspawn home as yet another trophy for the British Empire. He dreams of being honoured as a great pioneer by "the London School of Eugenics", and retiring to a cottage in Western Victoria. These reflections are accompanied by archive illustrations of colonial officers storming the frontier, and video snapshots of Psurumin statues in Melbourne's civic centres.

Blakely is similarly befuddled about his German Nazi hosts, who are initially his captors. While cautious of them, he also doesn't see the Nazis as altogether bad. After all, some of them are fellow scholars – surely, they are too refined, too cultured, to be altogether irredeemable. "He doesn't see himself in history, as he walks through this place," Faulkner comments. "He doesn't see the Nazis as the people that we see them as." In this, Blakely echoes Dyer, narrator of Lovecraft's At The Mountain Of Madness, who comes to admire the star-faring colonisers his team unearth in the far south, calling them "men of another age and another order of being". But he is also an expression of political myopia and creeping fascism in the present.

The inspiration for Blakely came partly from Faulkner's own time in the academic world. "There are tonnes of people who are scientists first, and political thinkers 17th in their thoughts," he comments, recalling his encounters with Trump supporters as a student. "People who don't consider themselves political and then end up taking incredible political stances on stuff, until it becomes clear that they do actually have a political ideology, that's sort of formed by being around the people they're around." Faulkner's other reference points for Blakely include Elon Musk, once "washed through the media as a green, eco-warrior guy", latterly an advocate for 'great replacement' theories and far-right uprisings.

Faulkner says that Penguin Colony's anti-fascist sentiments are especially aimed at "the rise of gen-Z fascism", expressed in online transphobia and anti-Semitic memes. "There's been a huge uptick in people trying to vindicate Hitler, and trying to rehabilitate him in the eyes of this young generation," he says. "What they say is things like 'the painter was right'." Faulkner thinks that this neofascism has "petered out a little bit" over the past ten years, but is still on the march. Above all, he sees its resurgence in the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, and in the qualms many self-described anti-fascists have about condemning it.

"I and every indigenous person I know, in and out of the games industry, have no nuanced emotions about what is happening there," Faulkner continues. "We know what this is. Like, it's our family stories come to life. We can see what this was. We're not just hearing stories anymore. And we're not just noticing the violence happening to the indigenous people right now. We're noticing how the mostly white, non-indigenous people are still conflicted on it and confused on it, and they don't have clarity on this. The idea with this game was to really bring this into focus, because the games industry likes to say that indigenous people are welcome. And they want to welcome us at our events. What does that mean? You guys want us here to talk, but you're not going to acknowledge the genocide of indigenous people that's happening in front of you, that every single human being at this point knows about."

Penguin Colony ends with a statement calling out the games industry at large for holding its collective tongue about the Israeli military's brutal campaign, noting that such "cowardice" will be "recorded by the art that it makes". The flipside of that sentiment is that art can be a record of courage and principle, advancing and nourishing a culture in which xenophobia and colonial ideology are unable to thrive. I see this idea expressed, again, in the journey of the Māori group, who are equipped to prevent Psurumin's return because they have made doing so a tradition and a practice.

"They know from generations of story, that you have to do it," says Faulkner. "That it's a responsibility to do it, when it happens." Thwarting Psurumin is part of the Māori's creative lifework, part of their journey together. "It is the job of our descendants to carry forward the story of our resistance," intones one of their group, the game's second narrator. "To create song, dance and story, so our people move toward the light and away from darkness... Every 100 years, to compose new haka and follow new paths unknown to our enemy."

As a whole, Penguin Colony aims to be one such path away from darkness, its methods a mixture of bald and oblique, overt and covert. I have barely broken the surface in this piece. There's an angry hopefulness to the game that coexists with the spectacle of a distinctly 'double-A' penguin bumping and slithering along boulevards of blue-toned, recessed stone. The player is invited to participate in that hope by the game's closing "expedition" screens, which present all the lore you've gathered – including photographs taken by the Nazis, and textual fragments of devious origin – as a web of stars, floating over an illustration of the Zodiac.

The invocation of constellations is gently subversive because a constellation is an act of selective reading, stringing together sparks in a void. Treat the lore as something you can individually exhaust or "100%", as in many RPGs, and your selective reading will vanish into the mass of motes. Rather than 'completing' the star map in solitude, the game invites players to reach out to each other and compare their constellations – a homage to a "pre-social media" era when the distribution of information was less the province of monolithic digital platforms, and also, a framework for political solidarity. "As we live in a world which continues to push us further apart, we invite you to come together, talk, share, and interpret what you saw," the game suggests.

The call isn't open to all, however. Penguin Colony is consciously designed to repel those who might identify with its Nazis, appropriating the portrayal much as alt-right memesters sought to deify Anakin Skywalker, in the run-up to this year's US midterms. As a rhetorical apparatus, Penguin Colony is full of traps, easily overlooked if you focus on its headline politics. "We have a character voiced by a German trans woman – they can't enjoy it," notes Faulkner. "It just makes their skin crawl." There are many more such snares in the game. The commentary on Israel and Palestine, especially, pervades Penguin Colony in ways I don't think any player has yet discovered.

The lore of Penguin Colony also harbours clues about Origame's future "inherently indigenous" Lovecraftian games. The next game in that trilogy was actually conceived before Penguin Colony, and will be set decades from now. Faulkner envisages it as a loose retelling of Shadows Over Innsmouth, Lovecraft's story about fishpeople cults and miscegenation in a remote coastal town. "It's this idea of, what does Lovecraft look like in a future that we're heading towards, in the sense of social isolation and landscapes of small town decay."

In place of a Dagon cult, Origame Digital's next game will focus on groups of secretive violent bigots, with the player playing the part of a detective - a premise that, more superficially, makes me eager for a resurrection of the photography mechanics in Origame's reputation-making Umurangi Generation. As with Penguin Colony, the concept draws heavily on Faulkner's own life experiences.

"I grew up in a cattle town, and cattle towns are notoriously pretty racist places," he says. "The whole thing is when I left the town, when I was 18, just because I was going to university, I learned that the town had an active KKK [branch] that was being run out of the Anglican church. And this town is one town away from Grafton, which is where the white supremacist terrorist Brenton Tarrant is from – the guy who went and shot up the mosque in Christchurch. How does that happen? Where everyone knows about it, but they hush up?" The forthcoming game will look at how bitterness and neglect may give rise to such hatred, as local economies dry up and support structures are stripped away.

The second game will also take inspiration from the North American concept of a "sundown town", in which non-white people face violence if they linger outdoors after sunset - a vicious history also explored in Matt Ruff's HBO-adapted novel Lovecraft Country. "I went through a big rabbit hole on Youtube of hearing stories of people talking about, like, getting lost on the highway, needing to stop for gas, and then realising they had to stop it for gas at a sundown town," Faulkner explains. "They stopped there. They go to pay. And the clerk just sort of gives them a look, and then nudges over to them that there's a guy in the back of the shop just looking at them. And then suddenly they're followed on the highway for an hour."

The final game in Origame Digital's planned trilogy is far more formless, right now, but Faulkner has dreams of venturing into the realm of cooperative multiplayer. "It's not even written down on paper yet," he says. "We've just talked about it. For one thing, I don't know if I've got the skills to do it, because Penguin Colony had some jank, and had some technical issues at launch, but I'm getting better at making games."

This multiplayer project would build on Penguin Colony's premise of playing a colony, hopping between penguin bodies while shadowing Blakely's expedition. It would also follow through on the former game's closing encouragement to make allies against inhumanity via the collective interpretation of a celestial expanse of lore. "It's about the whole group, and I think if the third one was going to make a point about coming together to solve the problem… you probably want to make that a mechanical issue," Faulkner speculates, "where we have to actually make players do these sorts of actions together."

#3758. Crusader Kings publishers Paradox announce CEO swap, say they're "in a strong position at a time when much of the industry is facing major challenges"

"My plan was never to be CEO for life", says man clearly not embracing the grand strategy despot spirit

Paradox Interactive, publishers of umpteen strategy genre stalwarts including Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis, and Hearts of Iron, have announced plans to switch overlords early next year. Fredrik Wester will make way for Mattias Lilja, as the deputy CEO takes the throne.

While the move's been announced this week, Lilja will properly become boss from January 4th, making this a case of getting a new figurehead in place as the calendars swap. Departing CEO Fredrik Wester isn't going far, at least for now, as he'll "continue focusing on the company's long-term development as a member of the board".

"My plan was never to be CEO for life," Wester said. "The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company’s journey. Since I returned as CEO, we’ve streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over."

"The Board wants to thank Fredrik for his visionary leadership and outstanding contributions over these years," stated chairman Håkan Sjunnesson. "As a result, Paradox is in a strong position at a time when much of the industry is facing major challenges." He added that Lilja is "more than ready to assume the role and lead Paradox towards new gaming experiences that last for decades".

Lilja himself declared that Paradox have "a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games" and will be "stepping up the pace". "We will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus," he said.

As Wester alluded to, he previously served as Paradox CEO from 2009 to 2018, with a brief stint as executive chairman of the board sandwiched between that and his latest stint as CEO since 2021. Lilja has been deputy CEO since 2024 and chief of staff since 2021, having originally joined Paradox as a producer in 2009.

The past half decade has been a very mixed bag for Paradox. Their big strategy flagships keep ticking along, albeit with the question of whether their next DLC will feel worth it hovering overhead near-permanently. Outside of that, however, the likes of Cities: Skylines 2, Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines 2, and cancelled Sims competitor Life By You have made for a track record heavy on questionable decisions and games which either flopped hard or failed to blow away expectations. Wester acknowledged back in 2024 that the company had "made the wrong calls in several projects, especially outside of our core".

With the likes of post-apocalyptic strategy game Afterworld currently in the works, it'll be interesting to see if Lilja's tenure can see Paradox finally start to nail not just their nerdy bread and butter, but also games that don't involve staring down at a big map.

#3757. Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Ascendance expansion may be getting a beta, some curious Steam backend updates suggest

Monster Hunter Wilds's first expansion, Ascendance, is set for release sometime next year. But, judging by some very suspect recent changes to the Wilds beta app on Steam, we may be playing some of the new stuff earlier than we thought.

On Steam, Capcom quietly updated the Monster Hunter Wilds Beta app to now say Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test. You can see the change log on SteamDB (via PC Gamer), which also shows an updated key art - all signs that point towards an impending beta for Ascendance.

The beta app is the same one those who played the original Wilds beta had in their library. Though the app was removed following the beta's conclusion, because the two share the same ID, the beta should be visible in users' list of played games under the new name. This could mean players won't need to sign up for the supposed Ascendance beta, seemingly only needing to download the new client.

Seeing as Ascendance itself doesn't have a release date, beyond a nebulous 2027 target, it's hard to speculate when Capcom plans to release the beta. Sometime early in 2027 would be a good guess, perhaps alongside a release date announcement.

Capcom has shown off Ascendance on multiple occasions, more recently in Sony's September State of Play, where we got to see a number of the expansion's new features. A few days later at Tokyo Game Show, we got a first look at returning Elder Dragon Teostra, which we can hunt in the expansion.

Capcom is keen for Ascendance to deliver the level of challenge Monster Hunter is known for, following feedback that the launch version of Wilds simply lacked that expected level of difficulty. While post-launch updates have certainly raised the level of challenge, Ascendance looks to be the next step up.

I reported earlier this week on a bug within AMD's GPU driver suite, wherein a misfiring utility was accused of making huge amounts of erroneous storage writes. Some AMD graphics card owners reported their SSD health dropping by up to 1% per month, but a fix has finally arrived.

AMD Adrenalin Edition 26.11.1 is an optional update, which means you'll need to download the installer yourself. However, according to the topline notes, the update fixes "excessive writes to the system drive" at idle for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and above.

AMD's wording suggests that older GPUs might not be affected by the bug, but some of the user reports mention RX 6000-series cards, so it's unclear if a fix for earlier models is still in the works.

I also think it's a slightly odd move to make this an "optional" update, given the severity of some of the reports, though this is often how AMD deals with getting fixes out in between official driver releases—by the looks of the known issues, this interim driver might still need some work before it's patched into the next full release.

AMD lists a litany of potential issues with various games, including crashes and driver timeouts in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, War Thunder, and Cyberpunk 2077 with FSR enabled. These issues, however, match and are fewer than in the previous driver release, with the exception of the Phantom Blade Zero bug.

The company notes that "visual corruption may appear on character hair while playing Phantom Blade Zero on Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products." I'm currently working my way through PBZ myself, and the idea of turning down the quality settings on Soul's magnificent hairdo? Sacrilege, as far as I'm concerned.

Still, I'd definitely consider downloading the update if my SSD health was rapidly being eaten by a misfiring utility. Buying a replacement these days isn't cheap, so anything that prevents unnecessary wear and tear on existing hardware is a-okay with me.

#3755. Ads are coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and an executive thinks this is the only way to avoid ‘dramatic’ price increases in the industry

Advertisements in subscription services are nothing new. Netflix, Amazon, and every other company out there has some sort of ad-supported tier, which is often way cheaper or even entirely free depending on the service and how aggressive the ads are. However, gaming is a different beast, and we companies haven’t found ways to implement them outside the mobile space, where they remain on a quid-pro-quo basis anyway.

But that is slowly changing with the prevalence of subscriptions, and Xbox Cloud Gaming has just received an ad-based free edition players can hop onto without paying a single dime. Xbox Cloud Gaming has long been in decline and probably quite expensive for Microsoft to run and sustain, which led to time limits implemented across every Game Pass tier. With ads, things could turn the tide on Microsoft’s cloud gaming service and, according to Xbox general manager Jonathan Stringfield, potentially avert inevitable price hikes throughout the industry.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Stringfield predicts that, in the coming years, the games industry will inevitably be faced with rising costs and sustainability issues, which will then produce “dramatic” results whereby the costs will be offloaded to the end-user.

“Either of two things need to happen if we want to stick with the model as it exists today: We either need to dramatically increase the price of games, which I don’t think would be terribly popular with folks, or we need to find other mechanisms to allow access,” Stringfield said to Games Beat. One of these “other mechanisms” is, of course, ads.

“When we talk about advertising—and things that are adjacent to it that amount to recurrent revenue, whether it’s subscriptions or otherwise—what this allows for is an alternative,” he explained.

Stringfield prefaced these comments by saying advertising definitely cannot work in every game and probably not even every console or platform, and it isn’t necessarily going to be hammered into everything under the sun. However, they are to be viewed as a potential way to offset costs without extracting more money out of the end-user via higher prices. The very existence of premium platforms, and quite popular ones at that, whose sole stated purpose is to delete ads, does run counter to this somewhat.

People are very obviously willing to pay not to see ads or be interrupted during their viewing or gaming, so it remains to be seen if or how advertisements can be used in gaming broadly, outside of the limited scope of ad-based subscription services. Maybe we will all end up on the cloud eventually (Sam Altman does seem keen on the idea) and thus be forced to watch ads and, like Sony’s patent says, even be made to stand up and scream the product’s name on the screen to be given the ability to continue.

Grim ideas, and I hope they never come true.

As the refounding theory finally starts to settle in, now we've got a shifting Great Calamity to deal with

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda timeline has gotten yet another confusing new update, shifting the events leading to Breath of the Wild by 9,900 years and directly contradicting established lore. It's such an about-face for the existing story that series fans are pretty sure it's just a mistake, but the new word comes straight from Nintendo of America, which is often treated as gospel.

The Zelda timeline splits into three different branches based on the end of Ocarina of Time, but those branches all converge in the misty history leading up to the events of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. Earlier this year, Nintendo updated the Japanese version of the timeline and made clear that the founding of Hyrule depicted in flashback during Tears of the Kingdom shows the start of a new Hyrule, well after the one depicted in Ocarina of Time and other games has faded into history.

Now, Nintendo of America has updated the official English-language timeline to confirm the refounding – well, I say "confirm" but I'm sure it'll remain contentiously debated among the most dedicated purists. Either way, the update has made another curious tweak to the rest of the backstory.

Up until now, we've understood the timeline depicted in Tears of the Kingdom's flashbacks like this: Hyrule is (re)founded, Ganondorf appears to invade, and is sealed away as part of the Imprisoning War. Untold generations pass, and the evil entity known as Calamity Ganon eventually emerges and ravages the kingdom before being pushed back by Sheikah technology. 10,000 years pass from that Great Calamity, and that brings us to Breath of the Wild. Calamity Ganon reemerges, Link hibernates for 100 years, and the game begins.

According to the new timeline, the Imprisoning War happens, 9,900 years pass, and then the Great Calamity happens. Then it's just 100 years before Ganon reemerges – now referred to as "the second Great Calamity" – kicking off Link's century-long hibernation leading into Breath of the Wild.

In other words, the first Great Calamity, which was originally placed 10,000 years before Breath of the Wild, now takes place just a century or two before the game's events. This is despite the fact that Breath of the Wild is full of people trying to unlock the secrets of a pre-Calamity world that's long since faded into myth.

How are Zelda fans taking the sudden break in established lore? Well, you can read the Reddit threads for yourself, but I imagine you can already guess the tone of the responses. The Zelda timeline is notoriously convoluted, and while Nintendo has kept it up since at least 2003, Shigeru Miyamoto always maintained that it's "not that important to us."

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Perhaps that's why Eiji Aonuma shut down attempts to add further nods to the timeline Ocarina of Time, and why a new official timeline update can so suddenly make an astronomical shift to established lore. Don't worry – regardless of how this detail shakes out, I'm sure the timeline will be broken in all-new ways soon enough.

Nintendo pulled back the horror from one of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake's most terrifying enemies: "Maybe we've gone a step too far."

#3753. Worst Class Ever takes asymmetrical multiplayer back to school, with a teacher player trying to spot the naughty children among the NPCs

Master the sinful art of eating sweets behind your textbook

What's the best prank you ever pulled on a teacher in school, assuming you went to school? By which I mean, a genuinely funny prank that didn't cause any injuries, break any of the more important laws (legal or ethical), or leave anybody with years of mental distress.

I'll start: I once had to write a four-page punishment essay with the topic "silence is golden", after being caught talking in class. I took the essay very seriously for the first three pages, only to end it with the phrase "...but not as golden as my arse." The teacher who set me the essay smugly tore it up without reading it - as I knew he would. Checkmate, Mr Thompson. Decades later, the last laugh remains mine.

Worst Class Ever is a new don't-call-it-friendslop asymmetrical multiplayer game dedicated to such larks. One player is a teacher, and seven others are naughty delinquent children, hiding in amongst some well-brought-up and obedient NPCs. As the wayward tykes, your goal is to do mischievous things like eating at your desk, passing notes, dropping banana skins, and playing on your phone, without being spotted by Teach.

All of this takes place in a breezy modern Japanese high school, the kind familiar from a million animes. Bagsy the Protagonist Desk by the window at the back of the class! The maplist spans the curriculum, from computer labs to gym tracks to stepped lecture theatres. I don't think there are any covert edu-tainment mechanics, but if you're playing Teacher, I guess there's nothing to stop you actually explaining the periodic table while trying to work out who keeps throwing chalk at your head.

What a wholesome and whimsical place! Such happy memories! Oh crikey, the male teacher is terrifying – why can't he stop grinning? And why do I have a smoke grenade? Why is this lesson taking place in the dark? Why are the teachers permitted to punch the students and tie them to wooden posts? Worst Class Ever definitely isn't a horror game, but I'm not sure I'd send my kids to this particular institution. I feel like we're one texture pack away from playing a more sociable version of Little Nightmares. Read more on Steam.

#3752. World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunters have found the MMO's first hidden treasure

World of Warcraft secret hunters are a noble breed, known for scouring the MMO for years for hidden trinkets and treasures. With World of Warcraft: Forever's launch, they've uncovered a quest chain for an especially fancy sword.

Over the past week, members of the WoW Secret Hunters Discord found a quest chain that takes place entirely on the Zephras Isle, meaning you'll need to have access to the Skyborne elves to grab this sword. Navigating the island, you'll need to first pick up an ancient heirloom ring from the starting zone. Simple enough!

Then, you'll need to head to Duskwood to gather the Night Watchman's Torch, a handy light source primarily used to light up areas across the darkened woods near Stormwind. It turns out this torch has uses far beyond this one zone however, as taking it back to the Ruins of Ban'aethal on the Zephras Isle will reward you with a secret quest and the Ancient Hilt.

With the hilt and ring, you then must track down an Ancient Blade from one of several spawn locations on the Zephras Isle. Once you finally track it down, that's the end of part one of this quest chain. You get the sword: Eluvi'ana, which on its own isn't particularly strong, but is speculated to be upgraded later down the line.

You then need to get a corrupted water globe from either Darkshore or the Blackfathom Deeps dungeon depending on your faction, do a fetch quest for a hidden spirit in Ashenvale, then take your hoard of special quest items to a NPC in the new Shen'Dralar zone.

He won't give you the finished sword. Instead he sends you to gather more items from higher-level zones. You'll need to raid a secluded vault in Feralas that you can only see with the Ancient Hilt, dive underwater in Azshara, and kill Highborne Shades in Winterspring. Once you've done all that, you can then cleanse the orb up in Hyjal, speak to the fella back in Shen'Dralar, then shimmy over to the end game Dire Maul dungeon to speak to Prince Tortheldrin about *another* sword.

This is how far the World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunter community has gotten to. It's believed that grinding up the Shen'dralar reputation to Honoured is required for the next step, as Prince Tortheldrin pretty much says as much in his dialogue. So the hunt is still on!

These sorts of secrets make up an important part of any good MMO: the solving of mysteries in these vast digital open worlds. In retail WoW, I have fond memories of the Waist of Time quest chain, which was an arduous and comical grind for a fancy belt during the Battle for Azeroth expansion. This secret sword quest chain may very well evolve into something as legendary as that, at least I hope so!

If you're not already playing it, World of Warcraft: Forever is plenty of fun. A record-breaking number of players are making the journey through Azeroth right now, diving into quests and dungeons new and old.

#3750. While soulslikes went bigger than big, Death's Door swung open the appeal of a tighter adventure

Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones. Elden Rings and Silksongs, with vast kingdoms and deep, rattling toolkits for surviving them. The reason it’s a fool’s game is because you can also have something like Death’s Door, a taut, compact, lighthearted little actioner that fills eight hours instead of 80 and yet never feels underwhelming or compromised for it.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition. You are a crow. You hit things. Occasionally you shoot things. You collect the souls of a frog, a yeti, and a grandmother. Everything in-between directly relates to finding the errant monster/pensioner, or at a stretch, upgrading one of those four abilities.

Still, it’s clever with its limitations. Environments are small in number but vary wildly in tone and texture, and they tightly weave their paths into criss-crossing bundles that maximise travel – evoking the sense of a great, ranging adventure within relatively tiny spaces. The lack of a wiki’s worth of combat options also never becomes a problem, partly because it spreads out its spell unlocks, and partly because the smooth, flowing back-and-forths of its central swordplay are pleasurable enough to carry it anyway. Good bosses, too! They’re all characterful, memorable weirdoes who fight unlike anyone in their minion armies, and usually come with a hidden weakness to deduce and exploit.

Which is welcome, as these big lads and lasses do tend to launch difficulty spikes right up your feathered backside, and do so in a game that isn’t otherwise as fussed about trial-and-error pain endurance as some of its inspirations. They don’t, however, bring the mood down. At times, this tale of a pitch-black soul reaper working as an agent of Death (complete with an office of Death and embittered co-workers of Death) can get downright cosy, leading through you through warmly-lit jungles and breezy waterside ruins.

Recently replaying, I’d also forgotten how witty it can be. Little gaglets are sprinkled throughout, both visual and verbal, but the best jokes are saved for – funnily enough – the bosses, who’ll raise your pre-fight spirit with some amusingly terrible trash talk before becoming the punchline themselves. I audibly wheezed the first time a death animation immediately cut to the foe’s impromptu funeral, their beaked killer among the precious few guests. And even when the joke is recycled later, I couldn’t help tittering at the sight of my enemy – who seconds earlier, had been attempting to fatally sit on me – lying nobly in state.

I previously considered ending my Valor Mortis review by calling it a gateway into the more demanding side of action-RPGs; a shorter, simpler alternative to FromSoft’s overwhelming titans that might nonetheless serve to introduce curious newcomers to their shared quirks and qualities. The game equivalent of splashing your chest with water before jumping into a pool. In hindsight, Death’s Door was always a better fit for that description, though there’s enough else here you don’t need to be prepping for something tougher to appreciate its lean, keen adventuring.

#3749. As of this week, PlayStation 5 has surpassed 100 million consoles sold

PlayStation 5 has officially surpassed 100m consoles sold, Sony's updated sales data revealed. The milestone was reached on 10th November, almost exactly six years on from the console's launch.

The figure represents 'sell-in' units, meaning those shipped to retailers, as opposed to 'sell-through' which tracks consoles actually sold to consumers. In other words, the number of PS5s in people's homes is smaller than that 100m.

Nevertheless, this is an impressive achievement, and gets the PS5 ever closer to the PS4's 117m, which it achieved by June 2022. It also means the PS5 has almost matched the original PlayStation in units sold (102.4m). As impressive as the numbers are, historical data shows that PS5 sales have been in decline.

Sony hasn't shied away from discussing that fact in its earnings reports. 2.6m PS5 consoles were sold during the most recent quarter (Q2 of FY2026), well below the 4m sold over the same period the year prior. In fact, Q2 of FY2026 is the lowest second quarter on record in terms of units sold since the PS5's launch.

However, it's also worth noting that, small though it may be, the second quarter's result is higher than the first quarter's 1.6m, the second-lowest of any single quarter since the PS5's launch, beaten only by Q4 of FY2025's 1.5m.

If numbers don't recover in the third and fourth quarters, this may be the PS5's lowest year ever in terms of units sold. Although the second quarter's sales boost can be attributed to the high anticipation of Grand Theft Auto 6, the overall downturn is largely due to the console's higher price; Sony raised the PS5 and PS5 Pro's prices on several occasions since 2020. The company's bottom line, however, hasn't been affected much, as its plan to generate more revenue from its already-engaged audience continues to work.

#3748. ‘The name’s Cullen. Edward Cullen’: Robert Pattinson reportedly top choice for next James Bond

It'll be exciting to see how he pulls it off if selected.

Bond. James Bond. Two words. Two syllables. Sharp, striking, piercing your chest as soon as they are uttered. They mean a lot to many, and every so often they are thrown into the ether, like a phonetic parasite seeking their next host. Who will carry them for the next year, two, five, a decade? A hard question to answer.

But according to a new rumor, Robert Pattinson is the top choice to embody Ian Fleming’s womanizer spy, with Amazon MGM reportedly considering him their favorite for the role. As first reported by Matthew Belloni in Puck (via The Guardian), Pattinson was given “favorable contract terms” to play this legendary character, which would see him star in three movies rather than the four expected of other candidates. The actor would also be paid significantly more, which signals how keen Amazon MGM is to get his face and name associated with the brand and character.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Previously, it was claimed Callum Turner was in the running for Bond going forward, according to Deadline, with Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor also putting themselves up. That outlet did say four offers were sent out but managed to confirm just these three, and it would appear now that Pattinson was the ultimate contender.

Now, if you asked me, I’d say Turner was, at least in terms of physical appearance and stature (which, of course, is almost just as important as actual acting skills for a character like James Bond) suits the character much more than Pattinson. The latter practically kills every role involving strange, mysterious, and at times evidently neurodivergent characters, and while he did nail the strong, silent stoic in 2022’s The Batman, I still fail to see how he could handle a highly sexualized, outgoing, womanizer Bond.

However, Daniel Craig’s Bond was markedly different than what we were used to. He had a lot more depth and a broad, emotionally charged backstory that fundamentally altered how he behaved. The core tenets of the character remained intact, though Craig did give them somewhat of a sociopathic tone.

How Pattinson will play the character and what flair he will end up giving him remains to be seen, but I’m confident enough in his acting skills to believe just enough that he can actually pull it off.

AI-enabled hacking is only continuing to get more impressive, and more scary, as a French bank claims a hacking group has cost it €100,000,000 (around $110,000,000)—about one quarter's profits. So not much, then?

That's according to an interview with Julien Carmona of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa with the AFP, which Boursorama reported. Carmona detailed the hack in an interview, claiming it to be a "heist of a new kind", stating the company has the "dubious honor of being the first French bank, and I believe the first European bank, to be the target of a successful fraudulent attack." (machine translated).

Carmona says the hack is "unprecedented in terms of sophistication" and "technicality".

Effectively, the hacking group managed to create fake IBANs, including those from Fortuneo (a bank owned by the group), "to trigger payment orders from Crédit Mutuel Arkea's own account to external parties using instant payment systems". These, "by definition have fewer controls than on classic transfers."

Carmona did clarify to Les Echos that though they use Fortuneo IBANs, "Fortuneo's system, and therefore its customers, were not affected."

‼️ AI-enabled hackers pulled about €100 million out of French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account.Its chair, Julien Carmona, told AFP how. The attackers took material from a hacked supplier, used it to get into the bank and generated fake IBANs at its online bank Fortuneo.… pic.twitter.com/fduRERezPWNovember 13, 2026

Reportedly, the hacking group used a compromised service provider of some kind to get privileged access, thereby bypassing restrictions normally in place to stop this kind of hack. When asked by Les Echos why they didn't reveal the name, Carmona said, "This is a collective decision by the banks. This information is not in the public interest and could harm the security of the banking sector. Similar service providers could then be targeted."

Starting on Sunday, November 1, the hacking group apparently made sure "everything was done to circumvent controls, to make these illegitimate transfers appear legitimate."

They then transferred the funds to legitimate European banks, where they then took that money and spent it on crypto platforms. This hack wasn't spotted until Tuesday, November 3, when access to the bank's information system was cut off, but by that point the damage was done.

The French bank has since brought in crypto specialists, who reportedly spotted the abnormal transaction on Sunday and Monday "But, at that time, they themselves, and no one to my knowledge, made the link with Crédit Mutuel Arkea".

Carmona says the hacking organisation was "a very well-organised, very well-equipped criminal group" and "very likely aided by advanced artificial intelligence."

It's not yet clear what role AI played here, but it's particularly good at analysing data, and of course has found value in coding over the last year. AI was only recently used by a cyberhacking gang to target 60 firms a few months ago. In this Korean case, though, the gang only managed to make $210 in ransom payments before being caught.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has been in a bit of a one-sided beef with Valve co-founder and CEO Gabe Newell for a while now, lately about Steam's AI disclosure that requires developers to include a label informing Steam users of AI-generated content. Sweeney has had a number of complaints about Valve's storefront over the years, which makes sense as he owns one of its main competitors, the Epic Games Store, but he's been doubling and tripling down on the AI disclosure issue as of late. In a new interview, he not only sharply rebukes the AI label, but embraces AI in game development to degree rarely seen by him or other industry leaders.

Talking to GamesBeat, Sweeney gives one of the most bullish takes on AI generation in games I've seen in my many years covering this topic. Get on-board or die, is essentially his perspective.

"It's really clear to me that large-scale game developers–setting aside indies, where there's always going to be specialties and niches, large-scale game development will be totally changed by AI," Sweeney says. "Teams that don't adopt it will absolutely be left behind and rendered uneconomical, non-viable compared to their peers."

Sweeney says he's against any kind of legislation to curb the use of AI in game development in the US because it would give other countries the advantage. "Everyone is going to be adopting it," he says. "When one team can make a game four times more efficiently – 10 times more efficiently soon, perhaps – than another team can make the same game, there's just no possibility of competing the old way. No game developer has 75% to 95% profit margins that they can put at risk by not being as productive as possible."

There has been massive backlash to AI in games from players, voice actors, artists, and indie developers, but messaging from big studios and publishers generally ranges from cautiously optimistic to vocally and enthusiastically supportive. Meanwhile, a report from GDC found that 55% of respondents said AI was having a negative impact on the industry. Still, Sweeney wants to make sure companies aren't being bullied into choosing human workers over AI.

"Because there's a big resistance movement against AI that seems concentrated on trying to bully developers into not adopting it by attacking individuals, by review-bombing projects and so on, I've been trying to make my views known to as many game developers as possible," he says. "We have to power through this and build awesome games, use maximum acceleration, because it is a survival issue for all the companies in the industry."

Sweeney has called Valve's AI policy "abhorrent," politically motivated, and nonsensical among other things, and we can add another descriptor to the pile today: toxic. When GamesBeat pushes back and suggests Steam's AI label is there to inform players, Sweeney says he doesn't "buy it in the slightest," pointing to Steam's user review system as a means to let players know about "a game's quality, scope, entertainment value and so on." Ultimately, he says AI can be a force for good and bad in game development, and he sees Valve's mandatory disclosure as a judgment on the technology as a whole.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"You can build good games and bad games without AI. You can build good games and bad games with AI. You can repeat those distinctions for all engines, all development tools, all methodologies, all countries of origin, all teams and so on," says Sweeney. "If we were to identify AI as associated with bad games, that's just unfair to developers who use AI to make good games. It's a guilt by association pattern that all developers need to push back on."

Sweeney argues that Steam's AI disclosure is "being used toxically here, because it's absolutely being used by anti-AI advocates to undermine the reputations of developers and the viability of their projects."

Newell himself has yet to respond to Sweeney's many tirades, but prominent former Valve developer Chet Faliszek hit back in a YouTube video in which he called Sweeney's behavior "AI psychosis." Faliszek also argued that Sweeney was "treating all the players like children" and advised him to "act as a player yourself for a moment and go, 'What would I want to know about a game?'"

Why so many game developers don't want to use generative AI

#3745. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is getting three big updates with new starting scenarios - organ trading, junk empires and fine dining

Mucky and disreputable kiosk game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim is getting three big updates over the next few months that add extra starting scenarios, building on the existing wealth of goods, materials, vocations and techs. Those starting scenarios range from peddling human meat to running the finest cyber-frappucino stall this side of Tannhäuser Gate. There are no hard release dates, and the contents of each update may alter, but developers Questing Goose Studio have shared some rough timeframes.

Coming up in mid-December, there's the Junker starting scenario, which I assume is all about trading scrap, rather than being a Prussian nobleman. You'll get a bespoke perk, new items, and the ability to hire, equip and send scavs on expeditions. This update will also include some minor expansions for the Fence and Gunsmith vocations – the latter will be able to flog or otherwise make use of shotgun shells, 25mm grenade rounds and a tier 3 handmade SMG, alongside new armour.

Late January is when you'll "very likely" get the chance to be an Organ Dealer, care of the second major update. "Players will start by buying different organs and fulfilling specific requests, and will later be able to grow or print organs," a Steam blog explains. You'll also be able to filter blood and remove diseases, with different blood types having different value modifiers. How will you get your hands on organs? By sending horrible black market thugs on foraging "expeditions".

Last but not least, the planned April update will add the Street Food Vendor starting scenario. This lets you weave a livelihood around choice beverages and edibles from a range of cultures, supported by updates to the game's Aquaculture and Hydroponics tech. Sounds a lot cheerier than the organ trading racket, but then again, Probably Stolen will doubtless find a way to make it utterly grim. Guests at Sweeney's Cantina know better than to ask what our frappucinos are made of.

Are you playing Probably Stolen? It's been doing better than expected. I was keen on the demo, but my attention was lured away by a truly upsetting game about dogpeople in caves.

#3744. "I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released" - former Tekken director Katsuhiro Harada trashes Microsoft's console in front of senior Xbox staff

Katsuhiro Harada, formerly director on the Tekken series, is known for not pulling his punches. This truth was reinforced recently, as he said he wished the Xbox Series S "wouldn't be released" at a developer panel. All while a member of the Xbox team was in the room.

Per Inven Global, Harada was sitting on a panel at the Console Game Developers Conference 2026 in South Korea. The panel was moderated by former Sony president Shuhei Yoshida, and featured Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee (Stellar Blade), Too Kyo Games CEO Kazutaka Kodaka (Dangenrompa), CD Projekt Red associate game director Paweł Sasko (Cyberpunk 2077), Ludeon Studios CEO Tynan Sylvester (Rimworld), and of course CEO of the newly formed VS Studio Katsuhiro Harada (Tekken).

The panel were asked about the advantages of console development, as well as specific challenges when creating games for certain platforms. Harada led the charge, speaking to the advantages consoles provide for fighting game developers, as the hardware is ideal for tournaments and esports events. Following this, he took an opportunity to speak about a console that drew his ire.

"That said, there's something I really want to say while I have the floor. Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released," Harada said (translations to English via Inven Global). Harada then asked Sasko from the CD Projekt Red team whether he was "upset inside" because of the Xbox Series S.

Sasko proceeded to "burst out laughing" according to Inven Global, before responding: "It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly."

Harada followed up with additional thoughts: "You just used a very polite and elegant way to say "Xbox Series S sucks," right? (laughs) Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child.

"Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

Sasko stepped up to offer some perks to the Series S. While he agreed that many players the full technical context behind the Series S' weaknesses, he pointed out that optimisation for weaker hardware like the Series S made games run "significantly better" across all platforms. He even had a Cyberpunk 2077 example, as optimisation work done for the Switch 2 version were applied to all platforms "to great effect". Sasko also pointed to the affordability side of the argument, saying that the cheaper price of the Series S allows for market expansion.

Harada responded: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

Here, Shift Up's DongKi Lee ended the topic with some optimism for Microsoft's future consoles: "Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Earlier this year Harada founded Vs Studio with SNK's support, with other veterans from Bandai Namco's Tekken team hopping on board for whatever it's working on. As for the Xbox Helix consoles, in this current hardware environment with bloated costs for RAM and other components, it's reportedly looking a tad expensive. Maybe a Series S equivalent is on the cards?

#3743. New York City, Mayor Mamdani to host youth game dev contest to help boost local game industry growth

The home locale of Rockstar Games’ corporate headquarters is trying to invest in further game development locally, thanks in large part to a certain popular mayor and his office.

Today, New York City and Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced NYC Game Jam, a two-day youth competition for game development in which young New Yorkers “design and build a video game around a set theme,” according to a report by Variety. It will take place this weekend.

But don’t expect a return to Liberty City here. The competition’s theme is “Get There Already,” focused on the city’s transit, and according to the Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment, “participants will build a game about getting across the city” and “every game must be about transit or the experience of getting around a city, suitable for all ages, and free of violence, weapons, and other illicit activity.” No grand theft here.

The office also said that NYC’s gaming sector lists “about 7,900 jobs across approximately 380 firms and generates $2.6 billion in annual economic impact,” so this competition is an effort to continue that trend and keep games being developed in the city.

“Whether you’re exploring the forests of Hyrule or riding across the frontier at Nuevo Paraíso, video games invite us into worlds born from the imagination of their designers. And that creativity represents an enormous opportunity here in New York City,” Mamdani said. “As the industry grows, we want to make sure the next generation of game developers and designers can build their futures right here at home. This Game Jam is a chance to open the door to that industry for young New Yorkers, connect them with the people shaping it, and give them the tools and support to turn their biggest ideas into careers.”

A panel of industry veterans will select three finalists in the contest, with first place winning $3,000, second place $1,500, and third place $500, with the winnings to be split amongst all members of the game-making teams. It’s unclear if generative AI will be allowed in the contest.

As a native New Yorker, this excites me. I’d love more studios to work out of Manhattan rather than California, selfishly, because it’s less travel for me.

#3742. Hell Let Loose's original developers' Napoleonic-era extraction game, Hunger, gets December early access release, and an open beta this month

Good Fun Corp, the studio made up of the original developers behind Hell Let Loose, has finally announced a release date for its anticipated next project: Hunger. The extraction shooter-slasher game enters early access on Steam on 3rd December, and there's good news if you're eager to try it out before then.

Hunger's first and only open beta has also been announced, taking place 27th-29th November, the weekend prior to its early access launch. Unlike past tests, this one is available for anyone who requests access on Steam.

Though it may appear as yet another extraction shooter on the surface, Hunger offers more complex and intertwined systems than most. For one, combat has a focus on melee with only a few intentionally clunky firearms available. Though this is a PvPvE game, the vs environment side includes the sort of puzzle-solving, questing and dungeon-raiding typical of RPGs. The game's alternate history, plague-ravaged European setting gives it a grimey, steel-and-mud look few games have.

Beyond the in-match experience, Good Fun's ambitions extend to Hunger's MMO-style progression, its hub area with distinct characters and varied playable classes - all of which can be sampled in the upcoming beta.

Hunger just came off a very successful closed beta, which clearly didn't suffer by kicking off right alongside Modern Warfare 4's DMZ early access. Hunger is currently among Steam's most-wishlisted games, with over 700,000 wishlists, according to the developer.

The launch version includes three large maps, six playable characters, and five Mastery trees with more than 100 Masteries to unlock for your characters. Hunger has only been announced for PC so far, but will presumably arrive on consoles following its early access journey.

#3741. Cities: Skylines 2 goes free-to-play, but only for a limited time

Cities: Skylines 2, Paradox Interactive’s ambitious follow-up to one of the best city builders of all time, has gone free-to-play. However, this will only apply for this weekend, with the event closing in the afternoon hours of Nov. 16.

The free-to-play model has more than doubled the game’s concurrent player count, bumping it from about 8,000 to over 16,000, according to SteamDB. People seem genuinely interested in checking the game out, though its less-than-stellar reviews and horrible reputation still seem to impact players’ willingness to actually spend any money on it, despite numerous discounts.

Speaking of which, Cities: Skylines 2 is also 30 percent off, or more if you go for the bundle and already own the original.

Ever since its original creators, Colossal Order, gave the game up to Paradox Interactive and Iceflake Studios, the game has gradually improved in overall quality. Things are undoubtedly moving at a snail’s pace, with Iceflake doing as much as it possibly can to salvage the title and reclaim some of that lost trust from the players. Despite their best efforts and, of course, several DLC releases, Cities: Skylines 2 still has a “mixed” rating on Steam, meaning it cannot be featured on the store’s front page or get any of that juicy free exposure from Valve.

The recent reviews fare much better, though. With 72 percent of those being positive, Cities 2 thus holds a “mostly positive” rating in this category, but players still have a lot of bones to pick with the game’s many systems, namely traffic and simulation, whereby bugs and issues that’ve been there from the start remain in the game.

I, for one, was extremely excited to get into Cities 2 ahead of its original release in 2023. The original Cities: Skylines is one of my favorite games of all time, and certainly my favorite city builder, and its sequel promised to up the ante on so many different levels. I was chiefly enamored by how detailed the new assets were in Cities 2, how big everything was, and how that would allow me to zoom in and see the minutiae from up close, but my hype evaporated once I got my hands on it.

The jank was unbearable, and the faulty simulation meant the game lied to you all the time, feeding you false information to make it seem like simulation was happening when, in fact, it was all fake.

Iceflake has since fixed many of these issues, and I will definitely be revisiting the game in the coming days.

Ex-Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has again been summoned to United States Congress to speak with lawmakers. On the agenda are national security issues that may have arisen from his, and his company's, relationship with MegaSpeed, a Singaporean-registered company at the centre of a debate about China's access to high-performance GPUs; possible interference with US export control investigations; and chip smuggling.

“As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and Megaspeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately,” US committee chairmen Mast, Moolenaar, and Crawford say about the letters summoning Huang, Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter, and Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler to Congress.

“We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the chairmen say.

This meetings are to take place with the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, House Select Committee on the CCP, and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Huang and Teter's meetings are described as 'closed-door transcribed interviews', taking place on December 1 and December 2, respectively. Both parties are threatened with subpoena to force their attendance if they do not comply with the request. Under Secretary Kessler's invitation is described as a "hearing" and is much more amicable.

It's a marked change in tone for Huang compared to a letter sent by the chairmen prior to his resignation from Nvidia, which simply asked him to offer an alternative date should he not be able to attend. That focused more on Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former managing director of MegaSpeed.

The letter to Nvidia's counsel Teter outlines the more recent concerns of the committees:

"This letter is to request your appearance for a closed-door transcribed interview on December 2, 2026, regarding AI chip smuggling, adversary military use of Nvidia products, and recent public reports regarding Nvidia's interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving MegaSpeed."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

If that's not a big headache for Nvidia, its former CEO has also been called in for a hearing with the US Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. This hearing is led by chairman senator Tim Scott.

Scott also calls on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to attend a hearing. Lutnick is Kessler's boss, and has reportedly accepted Scott's invitation. Lutnick has come under some scrutiny as to whether he was too soft on, or protected, Nvidia.

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology. I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The American people deserve answers.November 13, 2026

And the democrats readying to take over Congress next year aren't happy with Huang, Nvidia or the supposed risks to national security, either.

There needs to be a full accounting of Jensen Huang, Nvidia, Megaspeed, and the Trump administration's actions in light of serious national security risks. We don't need to wait for Dems to take over Congress in January. At a minimum, Congress needs to be briefed immediately.November 12, 2026

Huang's hearing with the Banking Committee is set to be public, taking place on December 3. It covers the "significant national security concerns" raised by recent reports, according to the letter.

The BBC reports that Huang is willing to appear before Congress.

#3739. GTA 6 might be censored in Japan, if the game's smaller install size and lack of "strong sexual content" warning is anything to go by

GTA 6 is finally coming out worldwide next week, putting an end to a 13-year wait and at least one popular meme format, but the highly-anticipated game might look a bit different in Japan.

Now that pre-loading is live for the Rockstar Games mammoth, players across the globe can finally download the game and drool over its icon for the next week or so. But pre-orderers in Japan have noticed that GTA 6's file size comes to about 208GB on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores, versus up to 212GB in other regions.

As reported on by GameSpark and covered by Automaton, the game also received the strictest age rating from the Japanese certification board CERO - "Z" which is recommended for players aged 18 and over - but the listing notably doesn't contain one disclaimer seen in other international ratings.

PEGI and ESRB both warn of the game's "strong sexual content." Curiously, CERO's rating includes no such disclaimer. Together, some fans have taken the lack of "sexual content" disclaimer and smaller file size as signs that GTA 6 might not include some of the risque content we know it'll flaunt elsewhere in the world - based on NSFW leaks and a past rating that already clued us into the fact GTA 6 might be the first GTA to feature full-on sex scenes.

The potential regional censorship isn't too surprising, though, considering how trimmed down GTA 5's Japanese release was at the time. Rockstar had to remove and alter a bunch of GTA 5 scenes to comply with the country's normally strict content guidelines, including Trevor's controversial torture segment and multiple scenes featuring nudity. Baldur's Gate 3, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt and many more have been subject to similar restrictions in the past.

Earlier this week, GTA 6 became the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation and Xbox's history. That's also not a huge surprise, either. The juggernaut game's lavish marketing blitz took over London's Selfridges and Rockstar is even hosting an entire music festival starring a couple A-listers.
